title: Model variant fallback misfire investigation playbook
author: Samira Patel
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes the observable signals, immediate mitigations, investigation steps, and retrospective actions for incidents where Redwood's automatic model-variant fallback logic "misfires"—i.e., the routing or policy layer falls back to a model variant that materially degrades output quality or causes customer-visible regressions. The goal is to give operators and platform engineers a repeatable process to restore quality quickly, identify root cause, and close instrumentation gaps so future misfires are detected earlier.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to Redwood-hosted inference and Dedicated routing layers responsible for model variant selection and automatic fallbacks.
- Not applicable to customer-controlled private deployments unless they opt into Redwood-managed routing.
- Covers both degradations caused by wrong-variant selection (e.g., smaller quantized model returned) and failures in compatibility translation (tokenization, schema mismatches).

When to run this playbook (triggers):
- Alert: "LLM Quality Regression" fires (precision/recall drop vs baseline) AND the model routing change occurred within the last 10 minutes.
- Customer report: multiple tickets reporting incoherent/incorrect outputs across same request patterns within a 30m window.
- Automated QA: quality-gate evaluation for a rollout reports >5% regression on core prompt-set in the last deploy.

High-level response objectives (order of priority):
1) Stop harm: restore customer-facing quality with the minimum-disruptive action.
2) Stabilize: ensure traffic is routed to a known-good model variant and verify metrics recover.
3) Diagnose: collect telemetry and determine why fallback occurred/why variant selection was incorrect.
4) Prevent: close instrumentation or policy gaps and schedule follow-ups.

Immediate mitigation checklist (for on-call operator) — run in sequence until resolved:
1. Confirm signal: open the Quality Regression dashboard and verify which tenants/routes show regression.
2. Freeze routing decisions: apply an emergency override to pin affected routes to the last known-good model variant. Command example:
   - CLI: redwoodctl routing override --route <route-id> --model <model-id> --ttl 30m
3. If override is not available or slow, fallback to conservative policy: divert affected traffic to the "safety" tier (lower throughput, higher-cost) that uses validated model images.
4. If outputs are toxic or unsafe, enable immediate quarantine mode for affected tenants (return standardized error responses and open incident channel).
5. Notify stakeholders: post to #platform-pager and mention owner_team leads, product lead, and SRE. Use incident template.

Dashboard and alerting reference:
| Dashboard / Alert | Primary metric | Threshold / rule | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Quality regression heatmap | Per-route rolling quality delta (30m vs 7d baseline) | delta < -3% and absolute failure count > 10 | ML Eval team |
| Variant mismatch tracer | % of requests served by a variant different from configured pin | >0.5% unexpected changes in 5m window | Routing service oncall |
| Tokenization-compatibility-errors | Count of tokenization or schema mismatch errors | >5/min | Serving-runtime oncall |
| Canary-eval-failure | Canary prompt set mean score | drop >= 2 stddevs | Model-onboarding team |

Note on thresholds: thresholds above are guidance. Adjust per-route baselines and tenant SLAs. Use token-normalized metrics for cross-model comparisons.

Investigation steps (post-mitigation):
1. Timeline reconstruction (10–30 minutes)
   a. Pull routing logs for the affected routes from t-30m to t+5m (where t is first alert timestamp).
   b. Extract entries that show variant selection, policy decision, and explicit fallback triggers.
   c. Correlate with deploy events, config changes, autoscaler events, and capacity shortages.
2. Validate telemetry:
   - Check KV/prefix cache evictions and warmup patterns. Cold cache may cause fallback to smaller model variants or CPU fallback.
   - Inspect kernel metrics for contention that may have triggered automatic degraded-mode policies.
3. Re-run offline evaluation:
   - Reproduce a representative sample of problematic requests against each candidate variant in a replay sandbox.
   - Use identical environment variables and tokenization settings. Record scores and diffs.
4. Identify root cause classes (non-exhaustive):
   - Policy misclassification: routing policy incorrectly matched route or weight.
   - Capacity-triggered fallback: autoscaler evicted a class of workers causing fallback to a cheaper variant.
   - Model packaging regression: mismatch between model config (tokenizer, max_length) and runtime manifest.
   - Canary/QA gap: canary evaluation missed the prompt pattern that regressed.
   - Telemetry lag: metrics were stale and the decision logic used outdated performance numbers.
5. Artifact collection (store in incident bundle):
   - Routing logs, request IDs sample (min 100), model manifests, canary-eval run IDs, metric backfills, and any override commands executed.

Telemetry queries and snippets (examples):
- PromQL: Fraction of requests served by fallback variants in last 5m:
  sum(rate(model_variant_served_total{fallback="true"}[5m])) / sum(rate(model_variant_served_total[5m]))
- KQL: routing logs (Elasticsearch):
  event.type: "route_decision" AND route.id: "<route-id>" AND timestamp: [now-30m TO now]
- SQL (ORB telemetry):
  SELECT request_id, timestamp, model_id, fallback_reason FROM routing_events WHERE route_id = '<route-id>' AND timestamp >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 30 MINUTE) ORDER BY timestamp ASC LIMIT 1000;

Service and ownership matrix (primary contact for each artifact):
| Artifact | Service | Primary owner (team) |
|---|---|---|
| Routing policy decisions | route-orchestrator | eng-platform/routing-service |
| Variant selection logs | model-router | eng-serving-runtime |
| Canary evaluations | eval-harness | applied-ml-and-evals |
| Autoscaler logs | gpu-autoscaler | eng-infra |
| Model manifests | model-catalog | eng-serving-runtime |
| Operator overrides | redwoodctl | eng-platform/operators |

Escalation flow and SLAs:
- 0–15 min: On-call operator performs immediate mitigations and posts an incident summary.
- 15–60 min: If mitigation not stabilizing, page senior eng-platform PM and SRE lead.
- 60+ min: If customer impact persists, escalate to Head of Product and Customer Success for external communications.

Deep-dive checklist (diagnostic hypotheses to test):
- Hypothesis A: Policy weights drifted because the weight engine used stale performance data. Test: check the "model_perf_aggregation_latency" metric and the last ingestion timestamp.
- Hypothesis B: Model artifact mismatch (tokenizer version). Test: compare artifact hash and tokenizer version between manifest and runtime.
- Hypothesis C: Prefer-higher-throughput fallback triggered by queue buildup. Test: inspect queue length and continuous-batching metrics.

Post-incident retrospective template (use in the incident channel):
1. Summary of impact: affected tenants, routes, duration, and user-visible symptoms.
2. Timeline: short bullet list of key events.
3. Root cause analysis: the immediate cause and contributing factors.
4. Action items: owner, ETA, severity, and verification plan.
5. Monitoring changes: new alerts/dashboards and expected detection window improvements.
6. Follow-up review: schedule a 45–60 minute RCA review within 5 working days.

Suggested short-term remediation (<=1 week):
- Tighten canary prompt set to include defensive prompt patterns from customer reports.
- Add a fail-open guardrail: if fallback is selected, run a lightweight canary comparator that rejects variant if delta exceeds a soft threshold.
- Make routing decisions auditable: persist policy trigger metadata with request tracing.

Recommended roadmap items (quarterly / medium-term):
- Instrumentation: add per-variant token-level quality metrics and heatmaps for faster detection.
- Simulation lab: add synthetic failure injections that emulate the top-3 misfire patterns to the platform chaos curriculum.
- Policy verification CI: run a policy-runner that validates new/changed routing policies against an expanded canary suite before deployment.

Appendix A — sample fallback policy JSON (example snippet):
{
  "policy_name": "latency_cost_fallback",
  "conditions": [
    {"metric": "p95_latency", "op": ">", "value": 500, "window_ms": 600000},
    {"metric": "available_gpu_slots", "op": "<", "value": 2 }
  ],
  "fallback_sequence": ["gptx-8b-quant","gptx-8b-fp16-slow","safety-ensemble"],
  "auditable": true
}

Appendix B — runbook snippets: how to pin a route (redwoodctl)
- Inspect current route policy: redwoodctl route describe --route <route-id>
- Pin model: redwoodctl routing override --route <route-id> --model <model-id> --reason "emergency-pin-<incident-id>" --notify 1h
- Revert override: redwoodctl routing override --revert --route <route-id> --override-id <id>

Contacts and oncall roster (primary + backup):
- Routing service oncall: @routing-oncall (primary), @routing-senior (backup)
- Serving runtime oncall: @runtime-oncall, @runtime-senior
- Applied ML: @evals-oncall
